steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on efficient partially relevant video retrieval using large vision-language models and super images. Motivate the efficiency vs. performance dilemma, explain why sparse frame sampling doesn't work for this task, and present our QASIR approach with the zero-shot and fine-tuning findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- From text-to-video retrieval to partially relevant video retrieval (PRVR)
- The efficiency/performance dilemma of visual backbones
- Reducing visual encodings: sparse sampling and why it fails for PRVR
- Our idea: super images with large VLMs, two research questions
- Zero-shot QASIR and its findings
- Fine-tuning and hybrid QASIR and their findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- T2VR -> PRVR
  - explosive growth of web videos; T2VR = search videos relevant to a text query, lots of attention in vision and language (cite)
  - mainstream T2VR assumes pre-trimmed, short videos; queries single sentences fully relevant
  - in practice: untrimmed, long, multiple moments (cite) -> query about specific moments, not entire content
  - PRVR proposed (cite): retrieve videos with at least one moment relevant to query (Fig. 1 (a))
  - previous studies: link text query with dense frame representations (cite)
- Efficiency vs. performance
  - practical PRVR needs both computational efficiency and retrieval performance
  - challenge: encoding dense frames through visual backbones; more frames -> higher cost, esp. long untrimmed videos
  - previous methods: lightweight backbones ResNet152 (cite), CLIP-B/32 (cite)
  - limited visual representations vs large VLMs like CLIP-L/14
  - VLMs follow a scaling law (cite): bigger -> better downstream -> larger VLMs should help PRVR
  - but just swapping backbone: low efficiency, much higher GFLOPs
  - CLIP-L/14 (cite) 162.0 GFLOPs per image vs ResNet152 11.6, CLIP-B/32 8.8
  - dilemma: efficiency vs high performance with large VLMs
- Fewer visual encodings
  - efficient video processing (cite): sparse frame sampling by randomness (cite), motion (cite), frame similarity (cite); effective for T2VR, action recognition
  - optimized for short videos / fully relevant queries; not validated for PRVR
  - sharp performance drop for PRVR as sampled frames decrease on benchmarks (Section 4.4)
  - model must focus on local moments; sparse sampling may miss them
- Our idea
  - efficient, high-performance PRVR with large VLMs (Fig. 1 (b))
  - super images (cite): video frames rearranged in N\times N grid
  - visual encodings reduced to \frac{1}{N^{2}} -> large VLMs usable as image-text encoder
  - RQ (1): do VLMs generalize to super images for PRVR? (2) if yes, how to get efficient + high-performance method combining them?
- Zero-shot QASIR
  - query-attentive super image retrieval (QASIR): attends to partial moments relevant to query
  - finding 1: VLMs generalize to super images, promising vs fully-trained SOTA with conventional backbones
  - finding 2: grid size, image resolution, VLM size = trade-off between performance and cost; smaller grid, higher resolution, larger VLM -> better but costlier, and vice versa
- Fine-tuning / hybrid QASIR
  - fine-tuning QASIR: few trainable modules
  - hybrid QASIR: combine high-efficiency (larger N, smaller VLMs) and low-efficiency (smaller N, larger VLMs) models
  - finding 1: fine-tuning lets VLMs learn super images, comparable to VLMs with dense frames, lower cost
  - finding 2: hybrid minimizes performance drop of large VLMs, further lower cost
  - code released upon acceptance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Videos on the web have increased explosively, and text-to-video retrieval (T2VR), the task of searching for videos relevant to an input text query, has received a lot of attention in vision and language. Mainstream T2VR assumes that videos are pre-trimmed and short, and that the text queries are single sentences that are fully relevant to the videos. But in practice videos are usually untrimmed and long, and they have multiple moments. Because of this, the query usually relates to specific moments in the video and not to the whole content. To make T2VR fit a real-world scenario, partially relevant video retrieval (PRVR) was proposed. It aims to retrieve videos that contain at least one moment relevant to the query (Fig. 1 (a)). Previous studies proposed a method that links a text query with dense frame representations.

For PRVR to be practical, we need both high computational efficiency and good retrieval performance. For both of these, the challenge is encoding dense frames through visual backbones. The model has to encode more frames, so computation costs go up, especially for long, untrimmed videos. To reduce the costs, previous methods chose lightweight backbones such as ResNet152 and CLIP-B/32. This choice can cause performance problems, because their learned visual representations are limited compared with large vision-and-language models (VLMs) like CLIP-L/14. A recent study showed that VLMs follow a scaling law, where bigger models give better performance on downstream tasks, so larger VLMs should improve retrieval performance for PRVR. But just replacing the backbone with such VLMs is not desirable, because they are not efficient and use much higher GFLOPs. For example, CLIP-L/14 uses 162.0 GFLOPs to encode one image, which is much higher than the lightweight backbones ResNet152 (= 11.6 GFLOPs) and CLIP-B/32 (= 8.8 GFLOPs). So there is a dilemma between computational efficiency and high performance when using large VLMs.

One possible solution is to reduce the number of visual encodings. For efficient video processing, methods have been proposed that sample frames sparsely based on randomness, motion, and frame similarity, and they were effective in tasks like T2VR and action recognition. But these methods are optimized for short videos or for cases where the queries are fully relevant to the videos, so they have not really been validated for PRVR. Unfortunately, they show a sharp drop in performance for PRVR on benchmark datasets when the number of sampled frames goes down (Section 4.4). The reason is that the model has to focus on local moments in the videos, and sparse sampling can miss them.

- Our idea: super images
  - efficient, high-performance PRVR with large VLMs (Fig. 1 (b))
  - super images: frames rearranged in N\times N grid -> encodings reduced to \frac{1}{N^{2}}; large VLMs usable as image-text encoder
  - RQ (1) do VLMs generalize to super images for PRVR? (2) if yes, how to combine them into efficient, high-performance method?
- Zero-shot QASIR
  - query-attentive super image retrieval, attends to partial moments relevant to query
  - VLMs generalize to super images, promising vs fully-trained SOTA with conventional backbones
  - grid size, resolution, VLM size = performance/cost trade-off
- Fine-tuning / hybrid QASIR
  - few trainable modules; hybrid of high-efficiency (larger N, smaller VLMs) and low-efficiency (smaller N, larger VLMs) models
  - fine-tuning: comparable to dense-frame VLMs at lower cost; hybrid: minimizes drop of large VLMs, even lower cost
  - code release upon acceptance

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Videos on the web have increased explosively, and text-to-video retrieval (T2VR), the task of searching for videos relevant to an input text query, has received a lot of attention in vision and language. Mainstream T2VR assumes that videos are pre-trimmed and short, and that the text queries are single sentences that are fully relevant to the videos. But in practice videos are usually untrimmed and long, and they have multiple moments. Because of this, the query usually relates to specific moments in the video and not to the whole content. To make T2VR fit a real-world scenario, partially relevant video retrieval (PRVR) was proposed. It aims to retrieve videos that contain at least one moment relevant to the query (Fig. 1 (a)). Previous studies proposed a method that links a text query with dense frame representations.

For PRVR to be practical, we need both high computational efficiency and good retrieval performance. For both of these, the challenge is encoding dense frames through visual backbones. The model has to encode more frames, so computation costs go up, especially for long, untrimmed videos. To reduce the costs, previous methods chose lightweight backbones such as ResNet152 and CLIP-B/32. This choice can cause performance problems, because their learned visual representations are limited compared with large vision-and-language models (VLMs) like CLIP-L/14. A recent study showed that VLMs follow a scaling law, where bigger models give better performance on downstream tasks, so larger VLMs should improve retrieval performance for PRVR. But just replacing the backbone with such VLMs is not desirable, because they are not efficient and use much higher GFLOPs. For example, CLIP-L/14 uses 162.0 GFLOPs to encode one image, which is much higher than the lightweight backbones ResNet152 (= 11.6 GFLOPs) and CLIP-B/32 (= 8.8 GFLOPs). So there is a dilemma between computational efficiency and high performance when using large VLMs.

One possible solution is to reduce the number of visual encodings. For efficient video processing, methods have been proposed that sample frames sparsely based on randomness, motion, and frame similarity, and they were effective in tasks like T2VR and action recognition. But these methods are optimized for short videos or for cases where the queries are fully relevant to the videos, so they have not really been validated for PRVR. Unfortunately, they show a sharp drop in performance for PRVR on benchmark datasets when the number of sampled frames goes down (Section 4.4). The reason is that the model has to focus on local moments in the videos, and sparse sampling can miss them.

In this study we overcome these problems and propose an efficient and high-performance PRVR method that uses large VLMs (Fig. 1 (b)). Instead of using dense frames or sparsely sampled frames, we focus on super images, which are made by rearranging video frames in an N\times N grid layout. This reduces the number of visual encodings to \frac{1}{N^{2}} and reduces the low efficiency problem of large VLMs, so we can use them as a powerful image-text encoder. Based on this idea, we look at two research questions: (1) Do VLMs generalize well to super images for PRVR? and if yes, (2) how can we get an efficient and high-performance method by combining them with super images?

For (1), we check whether VLMs generalize to super images in a zero-shot setting. For this we propose a method called query-attentive super image retrieval (QASIR), which attends to the partial moments relevant to the input query for PRVR. Zero-shot QASIR gives two discoveries. First, it lets VLMs generalize to super images and get promising performance compared with fully-trained SOTA methods that use conventional backbones. Second, the grid size, image resolution, and VLM size are trade-off parameters between performance and computation costs. That is, a smaller grid size, higher resolution, and larger VLMs give better performance but need more computation, and the other way around.

For (2), we introduce a fine-tuning QASIR that has a few trainable modules, and a hybrid QASIR that combines high-efficiency models (larger N and smaller VLMs) and low-efficiency models (smaller N and larger VLMs) to balance retrieval performance and computation costs. The fine-tuning experiments give two findings. First, fine-tuning QASIR lets the VLMs learn super images effectively and get performance comparable to VLMs that use dense frames, while reducing computation costs. Second, the hybrid QASIR minimizes the performance drop of large VLMs and reduces the computation costs further. We will release the code when the paper is accepted.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the explosive increase of videos on the web, text-to-video retrieval (T2VR), the task of searching for videos relevant to an input text query, has garnered significant attention in vision and language [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. Mainstream T2VR assumes that videos are pre-trimmed and short in duration and that the input text queries are single sentences fully relevant to the videos. In practice, however, videos are generally untrimmed and long and contain multiple moments [8,9,10,11]. The input query therefore typically pertains to specific moments within the videos rather than their entire content. To fit T2VR to a real-world scenario, partially relevant video retrieval (PRVR) was proposed [12], which aims at retrieving videos that contain at least one moment relevant to the query (Fig. 1 (a)). Previous studies proposed a method for linking a text query with dense frame representations [12,13].

For practical use of PRVR, it is essential to achieve both high computational efficiency and high retrieval performance. From both perspectives, the challenge lies in encoding dense frames through visual backbones, which requires a model to encode an increased number of frames and raises computation costs, especially for long, untrimmed videos. To mitigate the costs, previous methods chose lightweight backbones such as ResNet152 [14] and CLIP-B/32 [15]. This choice may cause performance issues due to their limited learned visual representations compared with large vision-and-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP-L/14. A recent study demonstrated that VLMs follow a scaling law [16], in which larger model sizes correlate with better performance on downstream tasks; larger VLMs are thus expected to improve retrieval performance for PRVR. However, simply replacing the backbone with such VLMs is undesirable because they suffer from low efficiency and consume much higher GFLOPs. For example, CLIP-L/14 [17] consumes 162.0 GFLOPs to encode a single image, considerably more than the lightweight backbones ResNet152 (= 11.6 GFLOPs) and CLIP-B/32 (= 8.8 GFLOPs). A dilemma therefore arises in balancing computational efficiency and high performance when leveraging large VLMs.

One possible solution is to reduce the number of visual encodings. For efficient video processing [18,19,20,21,22], methods have been proposed for sparsely sampling frames based on randomness [18,19], motion [21], and frame similarity [22], and they have proven effective in tasks such as T2VR and action recognition. However, these methods are optimized for short videos or situations in which the queries are fully relevant to the videos, and they have not been thoroughly validated for PRVR. Unfortunately, they show a sharp performance drop for PRVR on benchmark datasets as the number of sampled frames decreases (Section 4.4). This is because a model must focus on local moments in the videos, which these sparse sampling methods may miss.

In this study, we overcome these difficulties and propose an efficient and high-performance PRVR method that uses large VLMs (Fig. 1 (b)). Instead of using dense frames or sparsely sampled frames, we focus on super images [23], which are created by rearranging video frames in an N\times N grid layout. This reduces the number of visual encodings to \frac{1}{N^{2}} and mitigates the low efficiency of large VLMs, allowing us to adopt them as a powerful image-text encoder. Based on this idea, we address two research questions: (1) Do VLMs generalize well to super images for PRVR? and if so, (2) how can we achieve an efficient and high-performance method by combining them with super images?

To answer (1), we investigate whether VLMs generalize to super images in a zero-shot setting. To this end, we propose a method called query-attentive super image retrieval (QASIR), which attends to partial moments relevant to the input query for PRVR. Zero-shot QASIR yields two discoveries. First, it enables VLMs to generalize to super images and achieve promising performance against fully-trained SOTA methods with conventional backbones. Second, the grid size, image resolution, and VLM size are trade-off parameters between performance and computation costs: a smaller grid size, higher resolution, and larger VLMs improve performance but require more computation, and vice versa.

To answer (2), we introduce a fine-tuning QASIR that incorporates a few trainable modules and a hybrid QASIR that combines high-efficiency (larger N and smaller VLMs) and low-efficiency models (smaller N and larger VLMs) to balance retrieval performance and computation costs. The fine-tuning experiments reveal two findings. First, fine-tuning QASIR enables VLMs to learn super images effectively and achieve performance comparable to VLMs that use dense frames while reducing computation costs. Second, hybrid QASIR minimizes the performance drop of large VLMs while further reducing computation costs. We will release the code upon acceptance of the paper.
